catalog_quote: Mandyali has three degrees of weight just like Hindi and Punjabi, namely light CV (L), heavy CV: or CVC (H), superheavy CV:C or CVCC (S). We assume without any argumentation that the S syllables are represented as virtual disyllabic sequence of HL as in Bye (1997), Vijayakrishnan (2002, 2007) ... This assumption allows us to classify the footing in Mandyali as a 'quantity insensitive disyllabic trochee' with feet aligned on the right (see Vijayakrishnan 2002). [p. 118] ... The stress facts of non-derived words which have not undergone any syllable augmentation/reduction are as in (18) below. (18) Stress in Non-derived Words in Mandyali: a. sa'bu:t̪ L(S) 'evidence'; b. bar'ba:d̪ H(S) 'destroy'; c. 'cʰalli: (HH) 'maize'; d. 'baḻgam (HH) 'cough'; e. 'ka:ṇa: (HH) 'half blind'; f. new_statements.quote: Stress: Stress as a distinctive phonetic feature occurs on vowels. There are three predictable variations in stress with which vowels occur (a) acute marked ['] over the vowel. (b) normal or medium stress unmarked [ ] and (c) lax or stress-less marked [ - ] over the vowel. [p. 26:] (1) The acute stress [ ' ] occurs on a vowel when the vowel is followed by an aspirated consonant or a glottal fricative and is not preceded by an aspirated consonant or a glottal fricative. ... (2) The lax variety [ - ] occurs on a long vowel when the vowel is preceded by an aspirated consonant or a glottal fricative and is not followed by either an aspirated consonant or a glottal fricative. ... (3) The normal or medium stress which is unmarked occurs on vowels elsewhere. ... All these three varieties are complementarily distributed and are treated as allophones of one stress phoneme.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only accessible first-hand description treats 'stress' not as a positional word-level prominence but as three predictable degrees of vowel prominence conditioned by adjacent aspirates: a vowel is 'acute' (high/strong) when followed but not preceded by an aspirated consonant or /h/, 'lax' (weak, extra-long) when preceded but not followed by one, and 'medium' elsewhere. No rule locating stress by syllable position or weight is given; the author adds that 'this analysis of stress is only tentative' and that stress, vowel length and aspiration interact in the syllable patterns. The pattern described is the aspiration-conditioned pitch/prominence typical of Punjabi-type tonogenesis in Western Pahari rather than a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author qualifies the whole analysis as tentative for lack of time and data, and notes that recognising phonemic stress avoids positing three contrastive vowel lengths (p. 26).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for vowels within the word ('a sequence of phonemes between two pauses'); elicited citation forms (c. 1100 words, 500 sentences, stories) from two matriculate informants of Purani Mandi, Mandi town, fieldwork June-July 1965 and 1966. Later census sketch (LSI Himachal Pradesh, Mukherjee) lists only length and nasalization as suprasegmentals and is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Ranganatha 1981 describes 'Standard Mandeali' as spoken by educated speakers of Purani Mandi, Mandi town (two informants, fieldwork 1965-66); this is the standard dialect of mand1409, not the North Mandeali / Chhota Banghali / Mandeali Pahari / Suketi varieties distinguished by Bailey 1908 and Grierson 1916.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule. 'Stress' here is a three-way vowel property (acute / medium / lax) whose distribution is fully predictable from the neighbouring aspirated consonant or /h/: acute on a vowel followed (but not preceded) by an aspirate or /h/, lax (and extra-long) on a long vowel preceded (but not followed) by one, medium elsewhere. The three are allophones of one 'stress phoneme', left unmarked in the transcription; the author calls the analysis tentative and notes stress, vowel length and aspiration interact in syllable patterns. Elsewhere (p. 84, morphophonemics) he notes that when intervocalic /h/ drops, the two vowels stay distinct 'by the stress that occurs on the first vowel of the sequence'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; analysis declared tentative for lack of time and data.
new_statements.identity_note: Ranganatha 1981 and Kashav 2013 describe Mandeali/Mandyali of Mandi district. Eaton 2008 describes Palampuri Kangri (Kangra district; kang1280) and states that no data on Mandeali, Chambeali or Kullui were collected. Thakur 1975's accent chapter describes Kului (Kullu district; kull1236); its Mandiyali section (pp. 90-92) has no accent statement. Also, the Eaton citation in the works list gives 'University of Texas at Austin'; the thesis is from the University of Texas at Arlington (hdl:10106/945).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Three weight degrees (L = CV, H = CV:/CVC, S = CV:C/CVCC). A final superheavy syllable is stressed (sa'bu:ʈ, bar'ba:d); otherwise stress falls on the penult, i.e. a right-aligned disyllabic trochee is built over the word with S counting as HL (so 'cʰalli:, pu'ra:ɳa:, 'kala:, and 'puɽija: where the final H is left unfooted); in an HH tie the leftmost is stressed (p. 141). Gemination, vowel shortening and unstressed-vowel deletion all serve to augment the stressed syllable. Non-derived words are at most three syllables; stress in derived words and compounds is left aside (fn. 62).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Mandyali (only for Punjabi, p. 117).
new_statements.exceptions: LH foot allowed only in disyllables; LL foot only with non-geminating intervocalic consonants; derived words and compounds not treated.
new_statements.identity_note: Ranganatha 1981 and Kashav 2013 describe Mandeali/Mandyali of Mandi district. Eaton 2008 describes Palampuri Kangri (Kangra district; kang1280) and states that no data on Mandeali, Chambeali or Kullui were collected. Thakur 1975's accent chapter describes Kului (Kullu district; kull1236); its Mandiyali section (pp. 90-92) has no accent statement. Also, the Eaton citation in the works list gives 'University of Texas at Austin'; the thesis is from the University of Texas at Arlington (hdl:10106/945).

readall_conflicts: Ranganatha 1981 and Kashav 2013 describe stress in Mandeali in incompatible ways, though not as a placement disagreement: Ranganatha (pp. 25-26) treats 'stress' as three complementarily distributed vowel allophones conditioned by a neighbouring aspirate or /h/, gives no positional rule and calls his own analysis tentative, whereas Kashav (pp. 121-122, 141, 145) gives a positional, weight-driven rule (final superheavy, else penult; leftmost in an HH tie; no final stress otherwise). The two are best read as describing different phenomena, with Ranganatha's 'acute/lax' varieties being laryngeal effects on vowel quality and length rather than word prominence. Eaton 2008 (Kangri: rightmost heavy in the stem, else initial) and Thakur 1975 (Kului: second syllable, non-contrastive) are about neighbouring Pahari varieties and do not bear on the Mandeali placement, though both are weight- or position-based systems compatible with Kashav's picture for the group.
